title: Ang 361–365: Guru Amar Das in Asa
tomorrow: what did the fourth Guru write for Sikh weddings?

lines: A SEED IN THE PACKET STAYS A SEED.
cards: Gardeners say it plainly: a seed kept in the packet stays a seed. It has to go into the dark and come apart before anything green shows up.

Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, has his own version of that, and it isn't about seeds. His hymns in Asa begin on ang 361, and a phrase runs through his writing that sounds harsh at first: to die through the Word.

teach.h: SABAD MARAI: DIE THROUGH THE WORD.
teach.b: The phrase is sabad marai: to die through the Shabad, the Guru's Word.

teach.h: WHAT DIES IS HAUMAI, THE EGO.
teach.b: What dies isn't the person. It's haumai, the ego: the voice that says me first, my way, look at me. In Guru Amar Das's hymns, the one who lets that die isn't left empty.
That person comes alive to the Name and finds peace. Underneath sits an old human question: how do you get free of yourself? A neighbor tradition asks it too.

teach.h: A GRAIN OF WHEAT, IN JOHN.
teach.b: In the Gospel of John, Jesus says, in the King James words: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
Both pictures say something has to end so that something truer can live.
That's real common ground. And here's an honest difference. Christians read the grain of wheat first as Jesus himself, his own death and rising, which his followers are invited to share.

For Guru Amar Das, what dies is the ego, through the Guru's Word, while you're alive: here, now, at the next meal and the next argument. Each says it in its own words, and neither needs the other to be wrong.

how: Guru Amar Das's hymns, headed Mahala 3, are read in order in Raag Asa after Guru Nanak's; Sikhs sing them as kirtan, and the theme of the ego dying through the Shabad runs through his bani.

s: 'die through the Word' means giving up on living
what dies is haumai, the ego; the one who lets it die comes alive to the Name.
the Gospel of John has a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit
John 12:24, in the King James words: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die.
the grain of wheat and sabad marai mean exactly the same thing
both say something must end so something truer lives; Christians read the grain first as Jesus's own death and rising.

games.q: your group project gets praised, and the teacher thanks only you. two classmates did half the work. what fits sabad marai?
o: tell the teacher, right then, who else did the work.
say nothing; you were the one who presented it.
accept it now and thank them privately later.
games.why: letting haumai die isn't going silent. it's saying the true thing without me-first in the way.

practice: Read a hymn on ang 362 if you can. Then sit and let your head bow a little, chin toward your chest, shoulders soft: the posture of someone not trying to be first.
Stay there for the sit, and each time a me-first thought comes, let it go back into the ground.
